props.title: L'Age d'Or
props.initialSlug: Surreal tale of forbidden love defies social order

sections.content: Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí's L'Age d'Or (1930) detonated like a surrealist bomb in cinema history. This deliberately provocative masterpiece weaves a loose narrative about two lovers repeatedly prevented from consummating their desire, while launching savage attacks on bourgeois society, organized religion, and conventional morality. The film builds on the experimental techniques of their earlier Un Chien Andalou (1929) but adds stronger political bite and social commentary. Its shocking sequences - including a scene of bishops decomposing and a Christ-like figure emerging from a murderous orgy - caused riots at its premiere and led to a 50-year ban.

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through avant-garde cinema for decades. Its dream-logic editing and provocative imagery inspired later surrealist works like Maya Deren's Meshes of the Afternoon (1943) and David Lynch's Eraserhead (1977). The way it blends eroticism, religion, and social criticism laid groundwork for provocateurs like Kenneth Anger with Scorpio Rising (1963) and Alejandro Jodorowsky's The Holy Mountain (1973).

L'Age d'Or's political edge and anti-clerical themes would become hallmarks of Buñuel's later work, especially in films like Viridiana (1961) and The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie (1972). Its techniques for visualizing the subconscious and mixing reality with dreams influenced the entire French New Wave, particularly Last Year at Marienbad (1961) and Godard's more experimental works. sections.content: Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing from L'Age d'Or's fearless mixing of provocation, politics, and surrealism. Mulholland Drive (2001) shares its dream-logic and exploration of desire. Charlie Kaufman's Synecdoche, New York (2008) echoes its reality-bending narrative structure. Even mainstream films like mother! (2017) borrow its religious imagery and societal criticism. The film's DNA can be found in any work that uses surrealism to challenge social conventions.
